raw:
{
  "question_intent": "Assess bank earnings-call question and answer for BoE research",
  "main_topics": [
    "UK bank margin outlook",
    "UK credit costs and trends"
  ],
  "answer_completeness": "Complete",
  "response_stance": "Direct",
  "evidence_level": "High",
  "contains_numeric_evidence": true,
  "contains_forward_guidance": true,
  "narrative_alignment": "Aligned",
  "question_quote": "Two questions as well please. First of all you have given us quite a lot of information on the structural hedge and the impact on the UK, but if you could just, take a step back and look at the overall UK margin in terms of UK bank and what the outlook is for the next couple of years. And then secondly, credit costs seem to be coming in lower pretty much every quarter, at the moment, than your 50 to 60 base points through the cycle. Is that how you expect it to remain over the next 18 months or so?",
  "answer_quote": "So, I'm going to interpret from your question, that you want me to talk about Barclays UK. So I mean we're not guiding to NIM, we're guiding very much to net interest income, and that's really because we're growing both the numerator and the denominator. You know, we're growing our asset businesses, strongly as you can see, and depending, in any particular quarter, the dominance of either secured or unsecured, then that's clearly going to make a difference to that margin from mix. But generally speaking, we do feel we've got momentum in the margin that's coming not just from the structural hedge, and remember that's coming from the strengths of the deposit business overall, but also from the fact that we are growing assets and in particular, I do expect that the promotional balances that we've written over the last 18 months in cards are going to start to mature and they start in the second half of this year. But the, the greater bulk, if you like, the longer dated promotional balances will really pick up in 2026. So, I'm expecting that momentum to continue. But more importantly I would say is just growing the balance sheet overall whilst growing that margin, so you are going to see that continued NII momentum. On credit costs, the UK generally it's just very benign and customers remain very disciplined. We can see that in their actions in terms of their spending. Spending has typically been below inflation for, for some time. We're now seeing signs that credit card spending is outstripping debit card spending but that's a relatively new sort of over the last six months type scenario. And at the same time, through COVID, they very much deleveraged their own balance sheets and we saw quite a reduction in unsecured lending through the UK. So, all of that is going on in the background, but at the same time, you also see real wage growth. You see good demand for mortgages, you know, low, but pretty stable if not slightly growing HPI. So, all of the economic indicators are actually pretty stable. Corporate failures are not systemic, they're idiosyncratic from what we can see. So, there are really no signs of distress in the economy. To give you an idea, our UK credit card delinquencies across 30 days are 0.7%, and our UK mortgage delinquencies are 0.2% across 90 days. So, they're very, very low in historical standards. So, over time we would expect them to normalise and clearly we're going to see a degree of normalisation as we continue to grow the book. But there's certainly no immediate signs of it so I think the customers are in good shape.",
  "reason": "The answer directly addresses the questions about the UK bank margin outlook and credit costs, providing a detailed response with high evidence level, including numeric evidence and forward guidance, and is aligned with the question's narrative."
}
